lead: Spark timing is the instant the spark plug fires. Spark advance, also called ignition advance, is how many crank degrees before top dead centre (TDC) the spark occurs. The spark must start combustion early enough that peak pressure arrives just after TDC. As speed rises, the flame covers more crank degrees, so advance must rise. At high load, advance must fall to avoid knock. Only a few universities teach this chapter; every petrol engine uses the idea.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.8 and Unit 3 for knock.

blocks.text: Top dead centre (TDC) is the piston position at the end of compression. Spark timing is measured in crank degrees from TDC. Spark advance θ is the angle before TDC at which the spark fires. A 10° advance means the spark fires 10 crank degrees before TDC.

Combustion takes time. The flame grows from the plug and raises pressure. Peak pressure should arrive about 10° to 15° after TDC for best work. So the spark must start before TDC. If it is late, the piston is already moving down and pressure is wasted.

At high speed a fixed flame time covers more crank degrees, so the spark must move earlier. A sample linear schedule is 1000 rpm: 10°, 2000 rpm: 20°, 3000 rpm: 30°, 4000 rpm: 40°. Real maps are curves, but the trend is clear.

Too much advance puts peak pressure before TDC; the piston fights the flame and knock can damage the engine. Too little advance puts pressure late; power falls, fuel use rises and exhaust temperature rises.

Older distributors used centrifugal and vacuum advance. Centrifugal weights move outward with speed and add advance. The vacuum canister senses manifold vacuum, high at part load, and adds advance because the lean mixture burns slowly. At wide-open throttle vacuum falls, so vacuum advance drops and spark retards for high load.

Modern engines use an electronic control unit (ECU) with a spark map of advance against speed and load. Load comes from manifold absolute pressure (MAP) or air mass flow. A knock sensor, a piezo accelerometer on the block, detects knock; the ECU retards a few degrees, then advances back slowly.

items: Warm the engine and set the specified idle speed.
Disconnect and plug the vacuum hose if the maker states it.
Connect a timing light to number one cylinder.
Aim the light at the crank pulley mark and read advance.
Compare the reading with the specification.

blocks.text: High load needs retard to avoid knock. Low load needs more advance because the mixture is lean and slow. Spark advance is scheduled, never fixed.

figure.caption: The line is the sample schedule: 10° at 1000 rpm, 40° at 4000 rpm. Notice that advance rises with speed.

spec.aria: A line graph of spark advance against engine speed, rising from ten degrees at one thousand rpm to forty degrees at four thousand rpm.

examples.question: A linear spark schedule gives 10° advance at 1000 rpm and 30° at 3000 rpm. Find the slope in degrees per rpm and the advance at 2500 rpm.
steps: Given N₀ = 1000 rpm, θ₀ = 10°, N₁ = 3000 rpm, θ₁ = 30°.
examples.answer: The slope is 0.01° per rpm and the advance at 2500 rpm is 25°.
examples.check:
theta0 = 10.0
theta1 = 30.0
N0 = 1000.0
N1 = 3000.0
N = 2500.0
slope = (theta1 - theta0) / (N1 - N0)
advance = theta0 + (N - N0) * slope
print(slope)
print(advance)

traps: Advance is not fixed; high load needs retard, even at the same speed, to avoid knock.
10° advance means 10° before TDC, not after.
Centrifugal advance follows speed; vacuum advance follows load through manifold vacuum.
For a timing-light check, follow the maker's idle-speed and vacuum-hose instructions.
Knock-sensor retard is temporary protection; the ECU then advances back.

quiz.a: Crank angle before TDC at which the spark fires.

quiz.q: Why does advance rise with speed?
quiz.a: The flame covers more crank degrees at higher speed.

quiz.q: A linear schedule has 20° at 2000 rpm and 40° at 4000 rpm. Find advance at 3000 rpm.
Why does high load need less advance than low load?
quiz.a: The dense charge burns faster and knocks easily; retard avoids knock.

quiz.q: What does vacuum advance do at part load?
quiz.a: Adds advance because manifold vacuum is high and the lean mixture burns slowly.

quiz.q: A knock sensor retards timing. State one benefit and one cost.
quiz.a: Benefit: stops knock and protects the engine. Cost: lower power and higher exhaust temperature.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production ECUs use three-dimensional spark maps with knock control and sometimes cylinder-pressure feedback. Research engines aim for MBT timing, the minimum advance for best torque. Search for spark advance map, knock control loop and MBT timing.
